text: A ten-minute walk lifts most people's mood, and it usually starts before the walk is over.

review.notes: Supported by acute-exercise affect meta-analyses; 'most people' and the low-to-moderate intensity case make the during-the-walk part defensible.

text: Standing up and moving for just a minute or two every hour can add up to real benefits across a day.

review.notes: Matches the sedentary-break literature and is hedged appropriately.

text: Stretching your arms overhead first thing in the morning can help wake up your whole body.

review.notes: Unevidenced folklore. 'Stretching overhead wakes up your whole body' has no mechanism and no study behind it; 'wake up your whole body' is not even a checkable claim. If the intended point is that any movement raises alertness, say that instead of attributing it to the overhead stretch.

text: Dancing around your living room counts as real exercise, not just fun.

review.notes: True and worth saying; dancing is moderate-intensity aerobic activity.

text: Climbing stairs works more muscles at once than almost any other everyday movement.

review.notes: Unsupported superlative. 'More muscles at once than almost any other everyday movement' is a comparative ranking with nothing behind it; stair climbing is demanding but is predominantly lower-body, and carrying, sweeping or swimming recruit at least as much. Either drop the comparison or state what stairs actually do (high effort per minute, legs plus heart).

text: Your body uses energy just to keep you standing, even when you're not moving at all.

review.notes: True; postural muscles and basal metabolism both apply.

text: Swinging your arms while you walk helps you move faster with less effort.

review.notes: Overstated and partly wrong. Collins et al. 2009 (Proc R Soc B) found arm swing cuts the net cost of transport roughly 7-13% at speeds of about 1.0 m/s and above, with no measurable benefit at slow speeds. It lowers the energy cost of a given speed; it does not make you move faster, and the benefit does not apply to a slow stroll. As written it claims both.

text: A short walk after a meal can help your body handle that food better.

review.notes: Well supported by the postprandial-walking glucose literature, and hedged at the right level for a nine-year-old.

text: Playing tag or chasing a ball is a full workout disguised as a game.
Moving around in the morning wakes you up, and unlike a hot drink it works on the way to being useful.

review.notes: The second clause is garbled — 'unlike a hot drink it works on the way to being useful' does not parse into a claim a reader can evaluate — and it smuggles in an unevidenced comparison against caffeine. The first clause duplicates SF-FCT-000003's territory without adding anything.

text: Drinking water when you're thirsty is usually enough — you don't need to count exact glasses.

review.notes: Audience mismatch that could cause harm. Thirst is a reliable cue for healthy children and adults, but thirst sensation is blunted with age, and this app is explicitly used by seniors — the group most often advised NOT to wait for thirst. As written it tells exactly the wrong audience to stop paying attention. Needs the age caveat, or should not be stated as a general rule.

text: Laughing hard actually gives your stomach and chest muscles a small workout.

review.notes: Hedged to 'a small workout', which is the correct firmness.

text: Your heart is roughly the size of your fist and beats about 100,000 times a day.

review.notes: Arithmetic checks out (~70 bpm x 1440 min is about 100,000 beats); fist comparison is standard anatomy.

text: Eating slowly gives your body more time to realize when it's full.

review.notes: Satiety-signal delay is well established, and the framing is about noticing fullness rather than restricting food.

text: Washing your hands well is one of the simplest ways to stay healthy.

review.notes: True and hedged ('one of the simplest'). Slightly thin on teaching value but it earns its place.

text: Eating fruits and vegetables of different colors usually means you're getting different vitamins.

review.notes: Defensible simplification, though 'vitamins' is loose — much of what varies by color is carotenoids, anthocyanins and other phytochemicals rather than vitamins as such. 'Usually' carries it.

text: A short walk outside can ease stress faster than sitting still and worrying about it.

review.notes: Comparative is a little brisk, but the direction is supported: acute activity lowers state anxiety while rumination sustains it.

text: Your skin is your body's largest organ, and it repairs itself every day.
Being even slightly low on water can make you feel more tired than you are. It's worth a glass before you decide the day is a write-off.

review.notes: Mild dehydration and subjective fatigue are well documented, and the second sentence is encouragement rather than a claim.

text: Spending time outside in daylight helps your body know when it's day and when it's night.
Sore muscles after exercise mean they were asked to do something unfamiliar. It isn't injury, and it settles.

review.notes: 'It isn't injury' is stated flatly and is too firm on both counts. DOMS is a symptom of exercise-induced microdamage, and more importantly the sentence is unqualified — it teaches a reader that any post-exercise soreness is benign, which is exactly the belief that gets a real strain walked on. The packet's own SF-FCT-000029 makes the correct distinction; this item contradicts the spirit of it.

text: Resting after a hard workout is when your body actually gets stronger.

review.notes: Standard, defensible adaptation simplification. Note it overlaps heavily with SF-FCT-000028 and SF-FCT-000030.

text: A short walk on a rest day can help sore muscles feel better than sitting still all day.

review.notes: 'Can help' is the right firmness for active-recovery evidence, which is real but modest and short-lived.

text: Muscle soreness usually peaks a day or two after exercise, not right away.

review.notes: Matches the documented DOMS course (onset ~8-12h, peak ~24-72h).

text: Gentle stretching after exercise can help your muscles feel less tight the next day.

review.notes: This is the 'stretching prevents injury' folklore in a new coat. The Cochrane review (Herbert, de Noronha & Kamper 2011, CD004577) pooled 12 studies including a 2,377-participant field trial and found stretching before, after, or both produces no clinically important reduction in post-exercise muscle soreness. Reframing it as 'less tight' rather than 'less sore' does not rescue the claim — there is no evidence for a next-day tightness benefit either. The claim itself is the problem, not the wording.

text: Taking a full day off once in a while helps your body keep up with everything else you do.

review.notes: Teaches nothing. 'Helps your body keep up with everything else you do' names no mechanism, no timeframe and no observable effect, and it is the third near-identical rest-day item in this block (022, 028, 030). A true but empty item is still a failure under the rubric.

text: Warm water on tired muscles can help them relax faster.

review.notes: 'Relax faster' is a comparative with no stated comparator and weak evidence behind it. Systematic reviews of post-exercise heat and warm-water immersion show modest and mixed effects on soreness and recovery, with no clear advantage over passive rest. Also, given a nine-year-old audience, a claim about hot water should not be issued without a temperature caution.

text: Your body repairs muscle while you rest, not while you're still exercising.

review.notes: The negation is false. Muscle protein synthesis and the repair/adaptation signalling cascade begin during and immediately after exercise, not only once you stop; 'not while you're still exercising' asserts a hard boundary that does not exist. It is also a near-duplicate of SF-FCT-000022, which makes the same point without the false half.

text: Feeling tired after a workout is normal — feeling sharp pain is not.

review.notes: Genuinely useful safety content, correctly firm.

text: Giving your body a break after a busy week helps it come back stronger for the next one.

review.notes: Motivational filler, not a fact. 'Come back stronger for the next one' restates SF-FCT-000022 and SF-FCT-000026 with no added content and no mechanism a reader learns anything from.

text: Most of your body's repair work happens while you're asleep.

review.notes: 'Most' is an unquantified proportional claim nobody has measured. Tissue repair runs around the clock; what is supported is that some repair-related processes (growth hormone release, elevated protein synthesis) are concentrated in deep sleep. State that instead of a share of the total.

text: A consistent bedtime helps, because your body starts getting ready for sleep before you do — but it doesn't buy you fewer hours.

review.notes: Good — the 'doesn't buy you fewer hours' clause is exactly the kind of honest limit the library needs more of.

text: Bright screens before bed can trick your brain into thinking it's still daytime.

review.notes: Melatonin suppression by evening light is established; 'can trick' is the right firmness given that device-screen effect sizes are debated.

text: Your brain sorts and stores memories while you sleep.
A short nap can make you feel more focused without ruining your night's sleep.

review.notes: The condition that makes this true is missing. Short naps do not disrupt night sleep when taken in the early afternoon; naps taken late in the day, or long ones, demonstrably do. The item states 'without ruining your night's sleep' flatly while omitting the timing caveat, so a reader who naps at 6pm has been misinformed by it.

text: A cooler room tends to help most people fall asleep faster.

review.notes: Supported by the thermoregulatory sleep-onset literature and hedged to 'most people'.

text: Kids and teens usually need more sleep than adults because their bodies are still growing.

review.notes: The sleep-need claim matches AASM/CDC age guidance; 'because their bodies are still growing' is a loose but acceptable child-level reason.

text: Waking up at the same time every day can actually help you fall asleep easier at night.
Your muscles relax more deeply during sleep than at almost any other time.

review.notes: Imprecise as stated. The deep muscle relaxation people mean here is REM atonia, a feature of one sleep stage, not of sleep generally; muscle tone during NREM is not obviously lower than during quiet waking rest. The 'more than almost any other time' superlative is not supported for sleep as a whole, and the item teaches nothing actionable either way.

text: A short walk earlier in the day can help you sleep better that night.
Standing on one foot for a few seconds a day can quietly improve your balance over time.

review.notes: The dose is invented. Balance-training studies that show improvement use roughly 10-15 minutes of practice three or more times a week over 4-6 weeks; 'a few seconds a day' is far below any studied dose and there is no evidence it produces the promised gain. The activity is fine and safe — the quantity attached to it is not supportable.

text: Balance isn't just for athletes — it helps prevent everyday trips and falls.

review.notes: Supported by the falls-prevention evidence, and the 'not just for athletes' framing suits the senior audience.

text: Your eyes, ears, and feet all work together to help you stay balanced.

review.notes: Correct at a child's level: vision, vestibular system, proprioception.

text: Practicing balance gets easier the more often you do it, at any age.
Closing your eyes while standing still makes balancing much harder, which shows how much your eyes help.

review.notes: Safety violation — the rubric explicitly bans eyes-closed movement, and this item is an invitation to try it. It tells a nine-year-old or a senior to close their eyes while standing, and the fall risk IS the demonstration, so the danger is the point of the item rather than an incidental side effect. It carries no instruction to hold onto something or sit down. In a falls-aware app aimed partly at older adults this should not ship in any form; the same teaching point is already made safely by SF-FCT-000043.

text: Walking on uneven ground, like grass or sand, quietly trains your balance.

review.notes: True and appropriately modest; uneven-surface walking does challenge proprioception and balance. Descriptive, not instructional, so no fall-risk framing needed.

text: Balance tends to improve fastest when you practice it in small amounts, often.

review.notes: Distributed practice (short, frequent) beating massed practice is supported in motor learning, including balance-board studies spaced across days. 'tends to' keeps the firmness honest.

text: Carrying something in one hand can test your balance more than you'd expect.

review.notes: An asymmetric load genuinely shifts the centre of mass and loads balance; harmless and concrete.

text: Good balance helps with everyday things, like getting dressed while standing up.

review.notes: Standard functional-balance example, true and useful.

text: Toddlers and grandparents can both benefit from the exact same simple balance practice.

review.notes: 'the exact same' is stated far more firmly than anything supports, and it is the one item here with a safety edge: balance work for an older adult is normally prescribed with a hand on a chair or counter and fall precautions, which toddler balance play is not. Either soften to 'similar' and name the support, or cut.

text: Flexible muscles can make everyday movements, like tying your shoes, feel easier.

review.notes: True at the level given; a task-level benefit, not an injury-prevention claim.

text: A little gentle stretching most days works better than one long stretch once a week.

review.notes: measured claim 'better than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: How flexible you feel shifts over the day, usually easing up by the afternoon. It's a small effect — a stiff morning means nothing.

review.notes: Diurnal ROM variation is real (studies find peak flexibility around 16:00, stiffer mornings), and the item correctly flags it as small and meaningless day to day. Good example of matching firmness to evidence.

text: Holding a stretch for about 20 to 30 seconds gives your muscles time to actually relax.

review.notes: 20-30s matches standard guidance (ACSM 10-30s), and 'time to relax' is a fair simplification of viscoelastic stress relaxation.

text: Being flexible isn't about touching your toes — it's about moving comfortably.

review.notes: True and deliberately non-body-comparing; good framing for a mixed-age audience.

text: Cold muscles stretch less easily than warm ones, so moving around a little first helps.

review.notes: Muscle temperature does increase tissue compliance. Notably it stops short of the 'stretching prevents injury' folklore.

text: Kids are usually naturally more flexible than adults, but adults can still improve a lot.

review.notes: Hedged with 'usually' and pairs the age difference with an encouraging, accurate second clause.

text: Stretching after a warm shower can feel easier because your muscles are already relaxed.

review.notes: Passive heating improving perceived and measured ROM is supported; the 'can feel easier' hedge keeps it subjective rather than claiming a mechanism it cannot support.

text: Flexible ankles can make balance and walking noticeably easier.

review.notes: Ankle dorsiflexion ROM is a well-documented contributor to gait and balance, especially in older adults.

text: Yawning and stretching together is your body's natural way of waking itself up.

review.notes: States the function of yawning as settled ('is your body's natural way of waking itself up') when it is genuinely unresolved science - brain cooling, arousal and social-contagion hypotheses all compete and none is established. Either reclassify as `contested` and say so in the text, or rewrite to describe what pandiculation feels like rather than asserting its purpose.

text: Doing something at the same time every day makes it much easier to remember.

review.notes: Consistent cueing supporting habit recall is well supported.

text: Missing one day rarely breaks a habit — missing many days in a row is what does.

review.notes: Directly matches Lally et al. 2010: a single missed opportunity did not materially affect habit formation. True and the right message for a streak app.

text: Small habits repeated often tend to stick better than big changes done occasionally.

review.notes: Repetition frequency driving automaticity is supported; hedged with 'tend to'.

text: Putting your shoes by the door can make it easier to actually go for that walk.

review.notes: Friction reduction / environmental cueing; concrete and actionable.

text: Habits form faster when they're tied to something you already do every day.

review.notes: Anchoring a new behaviour to an existing stable cue is the core finding of the habit-formation literature.

text: It's easier to build a new habit than to break an old one, so replacing beats removing.

review.notes: The operative advice (substitution beats bare removal) is supported, and the premise is consistent with the finding that old habits are suppressed rather than erased.

text: A habit that feels too hard to start usually just needs to be made smaller.

review.notes: Framed as advice with 'usually'; low risk and genuinely actionable.

text: Most habits take longer to form than people expect — patience matters more than willpower.

review.notes: measured claim 'Most habits' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Celebrating small wins helps your brain want to repeat the behavior again.

review.notes: Reinforcement stated at a simplification level a nine-year-old can hold without it becoming wrong.

text: Kids are more likely to be active when they see the adults around them moving too.

review.notes: Parental modelling and child activity are reliably associated; 'more likely' correctly stops short of claiming cause.

text: A short walk after dinner is an easy way for a family to spend time together and move.

review.notes: No health claim to get wrong; concrete and usable.

text: Playing outside together counts as exercise for everyone, no matter their age.

review.notes: True and inclusive across the app's age range.

text: Grandparents and grandkids often move differently, but both benefit from moving together.

review.notes: True, and it frames age difference without ranking bodies.

text: Family game nights that involve standing and moving can be just as fun as the sit-down kind.

review.notes: Not a fact - it asserts a taste preference ('can be just as fun as the sit-down kind') as though it were information, and it teaches the reader nothing they did not already have an opinion about. Replace with something concrete, e.g. a specific active game a mixed-age family can actually play.

text: Doing chores together, like raking leaves or vacuuming, is real movement that adds up.

review.notes: Incidental/non-exercise activity counting toward daily movement is well supported.

text: Kids often copy the habits they see at home more than the ones they're told to follow.

review.notes: Modelling outweighing instruction is broadly supported, and 'often' keeps it from being a law.

text: A family walk is a good time to talk without screens getting in the way.

review.notes: Harmless, specific, and no claim that needs sourcing.

text: Teaching a younger family member a new movement can help you both learn it better.

review.notes: Learning-by-teaching effect, hedged with 'can'.

text: Shared routines, like a Sunday walk, tend to last longer than ones you do alone.

review.notes: Social support improving exercise adherence is supported; 'tend to' is the right firmness.

text: Babies are born with more bones than adults — many of them fuse together as you grow.

review.notes: Accurate: roughly 300 bones at birth fusing to 206 in adults.

text: Your jaw muscle can bite with a few hundred pounds of force — which is why people keep calling it the strongest muscle, though nobody agrees how to measure that.

review.notes: The number is roughly double the evidence. Measured maximum molar bite force in healthy adults is about 120-200 lb (roughly 400-800 N), not 'a few hundred pounds'; only rare outliers and Guinness-style records exceed that, and children are well below it. Also note many popular sources quote 120-160 PSI, a pressure, and the item has silently converted it to a force. The contested framing itself is handled well - the text does say nobody agrees how to measure it - so fix the figure (e.g. 'over a hundred pounds') and keep the framing.

text: You're slightly taller in the morning than at night because gravity squishes you a little throughout the day.

review.notes: True; axial loading compresses the intervertebral discs over the day. 'Gravity squishes you' is a fair simplification, not a misleading one.

text: Your tongue is actually made up of several muscles working together, not just one.

review.notes: Accurate: eight muscles, four intrinsic and four extrinsic.

text: Nobody agrees how fast a sneeze is: careful measurements land anywhere from about 10 to 35 miles an hour. The famous 100mph figure came from a 1940s mistake.

review.notes: The numeric range is well supported: PopSci reports a measured maximum of 4.5 m/s (~10 mph) and PMC8663001 (Building and Environment, PIV study) reports a maximum instantaneous sneeze velocity of ~15.9 m/s (~35.6 mph), so 'about 10 to 35 miles an hour' is sound. The second sentence is not supported as written. PopSci attributes the long-standing exaggerated figure to William Firth Wells and states it as '100 meters per second, or 224 miles per hour' -- not 100 mph. The item has converted 100 m/s into '100 mph', which is a unit error that happens to land on a different (also-circulating) number, so the sentence reads as sourced when the source says something else. PopSci also dates Wells only as 'a mid-century researcher'; neither source says 1940s. Fix: state the debunked figure as ~100 m/s (about 224 mph), drop or source the '1940s' date, and note the figure was inferred from droplet sizes rather than measured. Confidence 'established' is otherwise defensible for the range if both sources are kept.

text: Your nose can tell apart thousands of different smells without you even trying.

review.notes: Deliberately conservative - it avoids both the old '10,000 odours' figure and the disputed '1 trillion' claim. Thousands is safely true.

text: It's almost impossible to tickle yourself the way someone else can tickle you.

review.notes: Well established (cerebellar prediction of self-generated touch cancels the sensation).

text: For how light it is, bone stands up to squashing about as well as concrete. Pull on it instead and steel wins easily.

review.notes: The compression comparison is wrong in the reader's direction. Cortical bone is about 150-220 MPa in compression against roughly 20-40 MPa for ordinary structural concrete - bone is several times stronger, and more so per unit weight since it is also lighter, so 'about as well as concrete' understates it and the 'for how light it is' clause makes the comparison ambiguous as to whether it is absolute or per weight. The tension half is fine (bone ~100-130 MPa vs structural steel ~400-550 MPa). Rewrite with one clearly stated basis of comparison.

text: Humans are one of the few animals that can sweat over almost their entire body to cool down.

review.notes: True and correctly hedged as 'one of the few' - humans are effectively unique in whole-body eccrine sweating, with horses the usual other example by a different mechanism.

text: Over a lifetime, your heart moves enough blood to fill something like a hundred swimming pools.

review.notes: The unit is doing all the work and is unstated. About 200 million litres over a lifetime is roughly 80-100 Olympic-size pools, but a nine-year-old reads 'swimming pool' as a backyard pool, where the true figure is several thousand - so the item is off by about 50x for the pool most readers will picture. Say 'Olympic-size swimming pools'.

text: Walking is technically a series of controlled falls — you tip forward and catch yourself with the next step.

review.notes: Standard and accurate simplification of the inverted-pendulum gait model.

text: Your arms swing opposite to your legs when you walk, which cancels out the twist your hips would otherwise put into your spine.

review.notes: Counter-rotating arm swing does offset the angular momentum generated by the legs and pelvis, reducing torso rotation. Correct at this level of detail.

text: Going down stairs is what makes your legs ache the next day. Your muscles are braking the whole way, which is the kind of work they complain about later.

review.notes: Overstated: 'Going down stairs is what makes your legs ache the next day' names one cause as the cause. Delayed soreness follows unaccustomed eccentric loading generally (downhill walking, lowering weights, new activity of any kind), not stairs specifically. Also near-duplicate of SF-FCT-000130, which states the same mechanism correctly and generally.

text: Fidgeting — tapping a foot, shifting in your chair — uses real energy, and some people do far more of it than others without noticing.
Carrying a bag on one shoulder makes the muscles down the other side of your body work harder to keep you upright.

review.notes: Contralateral trunk side-flexors working harder under a one-sided load is sound biomechanics.

text: The first few minutes of exercise feel harder than they should. Your muscles want oxygen immediately and your heart and lungs take a couple of minutes to catch up.

review.notes: Marked 'established', but the cited source contradicts the firmness. Xu & Rhodes, 'Oxygen uptake kinetics during exercise', Sports Medicine 1999 (PMID 10368878) states that TWO COMPETING THEORIES debate whether oxygen delivery capacity or muscle utilization capacity limits the rate of VO2 rise at exercise onset. The item presents the delivery explanation ('your heart and lungs take a couple of minutes to catch up') as settled fact. Either soften to the observed phenomenon (VO2 lags behind demand at onset) or mark the mechanism as contested.

text: Pushing a heavy door, standing up from a low couch, lifting a kid — those are presses and squats your body already knows how to do.
Walking and running aren't just different speeds: in walking, one foot is always touching the ground, and in running, sometimes neither is.
Your calf muscles act like a second pump, helping push blood from your legs back up toward your heart with every step.
Swimming is one of the only activities where your whole body works while your joints carry almost none of your weight.
Bones respond to being used — movement is what keeps your skeleton strong, not just your muscles.
A bike carries your weight for you, so the same amount of effort gets you a lot further than running does.
Reaching for something on a high shelf uses your ankles, hips, and back, not just your arm.
Walking uphill makes your heart work harder even when you slow down, because you're lifting your whole body with every step.
Standing perfectly still is impossible. Your body is constantly making tiny corrections you never feel.
Gardening involves squatting, lifting, reaching, and carrying — most of a workout, just spread across an afternoon.

review.notes: measured claim 'most of' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Your grip strength comes mostly from muscles in your forearm, not from your hand.
A push-up works your middle as much as your arms, because holding your body in a straight line is its own job.
When you jump, your tendons store energy like a stretched rubber band and snap it back as you leave the ground.
Left alone, people drift toward the walking speed that costs them the least energy. Your body works that out without asking you.
Sweat doesn't cool you down. The cooling happens when it evaporates off your skin.
That's why humid days feel hotter — sweat evaporates slowly when the air is already full of water.

review.notes: Dangling referent: the item opens with 'That's why' but nothing precedes it. These are served one at a time, so a reader who does not get SF-FCT-000110 immediately before it is being told 'that's why' about nothing. Needs to be self-contained (state the evaporation mechanism, then the humidity consequence) or merged into SF-FCT-000110.

text: Your heart doesn't wait for instructions from your brain. It has its own built-in pacemaker and sets its own rhythm.
Goosebumps are a leftover from hairier ancestors — a tiny muscle at the base of each hair pulls it upright to trap warm air.
Shivering is your muscles contracting fast on purpose, just to make heat.
Your lungs contain no muscle of their own. The muscles that breathe for you sit below and between your ribs.

review.notes: Factually wrong as written. 'Your lungs contain no muscle of their own' is false: the lungs contain airway (bronchial) smooth muscle throughout the bronchial tree down to the terminal bronchioles, plus vascular smooth muscle. Airway smooth muscle is precisely what contracts in an asthma attack, so this is not a harmless simplification for a 9-year-old audience. The true claim is that the lungs contain no SKELETAL muscle and cannot move air by themselves - the diaphragm and intercostals do that.

text: Blood is red because of haem, the ring-shaped molecule that holds an iron atom at its center and carries oxygen around your body.

review.notes: Haem/heme as an iron-bearing porphyrin ring is correct. Note the British spelling 'haem' is inconsistent with the rest of the library's US spelling.

text: Hiccups are a sudden spasm of the muscle under your lungs, followed by your vocal cords snapping shut. That snap is the sound.
Your body temperature isn't fixed. It naturally dips overnight and climbs again through the day.
Your stomach does surprisingly little of the digesting. Most of it happens further along, in an intestine several times longer than you are tall.

review.notes: measured claim 'Most of' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Fiber is the part of plant food your body can't break down, and that's exactly what makes it useful.
Vitamin D is unusual: your skin can make it from sunlight, which makes it less like a vitamin and more like something you produce.
Chewing thoroughly makes everything after it easier, because your stomach has no teeth.

review.notes: The stated mechanism misleads. 'Your stomach has no teeth' implies the stomach does no mechanical breakdown, but the gastric antrum grinds food by muscular contraction until particles are small enough to pass the pylorus - mechanical breakdown is a large part of what the stomach does. The benefit claim ('makes everything after it easier') is also broader and firmer than the evidence, which is mostly small studies on bolus particle size, gastric emptying and satiety, not a general digestive benefit. This reads as the familiar chew-your-food folklore.

text: You carry trillions of bacteria in your gut. Most of them simply live there, and the ones that earn their keep do a lot of work.

review.notes: measured claim 'Most of' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Blushing is blood vessels in your face widening — one of the very few body reactions nobody can do on purpose.

review.notes: 'One of the very few body reactions nobody can do on purpose' is false. Nearly every autonomic response is involuntary in exactly the same way: pupil dilation, goosebumps, sweating, gut motility, heart rate. Blushing is unremarkable in this respect, so the claim that makes the item interesting is the part that is wrong. The first half (facial vasodilation) is fine.

text: Cold hands warm up during exercise because your body deliberately opens up blood flow to the skin to shed extra heat.
Your red blood cells are replaced constantly. None of the ones carrying oxygen right now are more than a few months old.

review.notes: measured claim 'more than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: There are five basic tastes your tongue can detect: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and savory.

review.notes: Fails the quality bar: a bare list with no explanation, no mechanism and nothing a reader learns beyond naming umami 'savory'. It also states 'there are five basic tastes' as settled, when fat (oleogustus) is an actively argued candidate sixth - if the item is kept at this confidence it should not be phrased as a closed count. Needs an actual idea attached (e.g. why bitter detection exists) to earn a slot.

text: A room full of people warms up because every body in it is producing heat all the time, doing nothing in particular.
Thirst lags slightly behind what your body is actually doing, which is why a drink can feel good before you noticed wanting one.

review.notes: The reasoning is a non-sequitur: a drink feeling good before you consciously wanted one is not evidence that thirst lags your fluid state. The item is also vague about what thirst supposedly lags behind, and in that vagueness it points at the contested 'if you're thirsty it's already too late / drink ahead of thirst' advice, which is not the current consensus for ordinary activity. Either state the specific, supportable version (thirst is often satisfied before rehydration is complete, and during hard sweating people typically under-drink) or cut it.

text: The soreness from a brand-new activity shows up most after movements where muscles lengthen under load — like walking downhill.

review.notes: measured claim 'most after' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Do the same activity again a week later and it usually causes far less soreness. Your body remembers the first time.

review.notes: Repeated bout effect, well established.

text: Muscles don't grow during exercise. Exercise is only the signal — the building happens afterward.
Light movement raises blood flow to a sore muscle, which is why a gentle walk often feels better than lying down.

review.notes: States a mechanism more firmly than the evidence supports. Light movement does raise blood flow, but 'which is why a gentle walk often feels better than lying down' asserts blood flow as the cause of the relief. Active recovery's effect on delayed soreness is modest and short-lived in the literature, and its mechanism is not settled. Drop the causal 'which is why', or present the walk as something people report rather than something blood flow explains.

text: Your body keeps running slightly warm for a while after hard exercise, putting everything back where it belongs.

review.notes: Overlaps SF-FCT-000135; consider whether both are needed.

text: Breathing hard for a few minutes after you stop isn't paying anything back. Your body is putting temperature, circulation and fuel stores back where it likes them.

review.notes: Internally contradictory. It opens 'isn't paying anything back', then describes the body putting fuel stores back where they belong - which is, in plain English, paying something back. The point being aimed at (that post-exercise oxygen use is not a lactate 'oxygen debt') is worth making, but as written the reader is told the opposite of the sentence that follows.

text: Tendons and ligaments recover more slowly than muscles do, because they get much less blood flow.

review.notes: Tendon and ligament hypovascularity relative to muscle is standard.

text: Ice feels good on a sore spot largely because cold quiets the nerves carrying the signal.

review.notes: Cold slowing sensory nerve conduction is a well-supported analgesia mechanism, and 'largely' is appropriately hedged.

text: An easy day between two hard days is part of the training, not a gap in it.
A single rest day undoes nothing. Fitness is built and lost on a scale of weeks, not hours.

review.notes: Consistent with detraining literature; timescale claim is correct.

text: There's a simple way to tell how hard you're working: if you can talk in sentences you're going steady, and if you can sing you're going easy.

review.notes: Standard talk test, stated at the right level of firmness.

text: Growth hormone comes out in a pulse during deep sleep. It's the same hormone that rebuilds tissue, which is a good argument for the early part of the night.

review.notes: The largest GH pulse does occur with the first slow-wave sleep episode; GH's role in tissue repair is standard physiology.

text: Joints are lubricated by being moved, which is why stiffness after a long sit eases within a minute of standing up.

review.notes: Synovial fluid thixotropy is the mainstream explanation; 'within a minute' is slightly tighter than sources say ('a few minutes') but not misleading.

text: Slowing down gradually at the end of exercise lets your heart rate come back down smoothly instead of dropping off a cliff.

review.notes: The stated mechanism is wrong. Stopping abruptly does not make heart rate 'drop off a cliff' — heart rate falls gradually either way (that is what HR recovery measures). The real effect of an abrupt stop is blood pooling in the legs and a drop in blood pressure, which is what causes the light-headedness. Rewrite around blood pooling, or drop the 'cliff' framing; as written it teaches a mechanism that does not exist.

text: The first session back after time off almost always feels harder than it should. That feeling passes much faster than people expect.

review.notes: measured claim 'harder than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Your body adapts to exactly what you ask of it, which is why a routine that never changes eventually stops feeling like much.

review.notes: Specificity of adaptation plus plateau; fair as a simplification.

text: Repairing muscle uses protein from food you've already eaten — the work continues long after you've stopped moving.

review.notes: Muscle protein synthesis stays elevated for 24-48h after exercise; no diet prescription attached.

text: Muscles feel tightest right after you've been still, which is why the stairs feel worse at breakfast than at lunch.

review.notes: Morning/post-stillness stiffness is a real and commonly reported pattern; heavy overlap with SF-FCT-000142 though.

text: A hard effort leaves you weaker for a day or two. Then the repair overshoots slightly, and you come back a little stronger than before.

review.notes: This is the classic supercompensation curve stated as a mechanical certainty for every hard session ('the repair overshoots slightly, and you come back a little stronger than before'). Supercompensation is a contested training model, not an established per-session physiological event — different systems recover at different rates and single-session overshoot in performance has not been reliably demonstrated. Either soften to 'over weeks of hard efforts and recovery you end up stronger' or re-tag as contested and say so in the text.

text: A week away doesn't send you back to the beginning. Your body holds on to most of what you built.

review.notes: measured claim 'most of' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Caffeine doesn't add energy. It blocks the chemical that tells your brain you're tired, so the tiredness is still there underneath.

review.notes: Caffeine is an adenosine receptor antagonist; the framing is accurate and useful.

text: During dreaming sleep your body is temporarily unable to move, which is what keeps you from acting your dreams out.

review.notes: REM atonia, correctly described.

text: Sleep isn't one state. Your brain cycles through several distinct stages, over and over, all night.
The urge to sleep builds up like pressure in a tank the longer you're awake, and sleeping is what releases it.

review.notes: Homeostatic sleep pressure; the tank analogy does not overreach.

text: Your body begins preparing for sleep hours ahead of time by slowly letting its core temperature drop.

review.notes: Core temperature begins falling roughly two hours before habitual sleep onset.

text: Morning daylight is one of the strongest signals your body uses to set its internal clock for the whole day.

review.notes: Morning light is the dominant zeitgeber; correctly stated.

text: Some people are sharper at night and others in the morning. It's partly built in and it shifts with age — it's not a character flaw either way.

review.notes: Chronotype is partly heritable and shifts with age; the non-judgemental framing is right for the audience.

text: Teenagers' internal clocks really do shift later during puberty. Early mornings are working against biology, not just attitude.

review.notes: Pubertal circadian phase delay is well documented.

text: You forget most dreams within a few minutes of waking, even ones that felt vivid at the time.

review.notes: measured claim 'most dreams' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: That falling sensation that jerks you awake as you drift off has a name — a hypnic jerk — and it's completely ordinary.
Snoring is simply the sound of air moving past relaxed tissue at the back of the throat.

review.notes: The mechanism is right but the word 'simply' makes a blanket reassurance out of it. Habitual loud snoring is the cardinal symptom of obstructive sleep apnea — roughly 2-3% of children and a far higher share of older adults — and this item, aimed at 9-year-olds and seniors, tells the reader snoring is nothing but a noise. Remove 'simply' and add a non-diagnostic clause (e.g. that loud, habitual snoring or pauses in breathing are worth mentioning to a doctor).

text: Even a small amount of light reaching your eyes can delay the hormone that tells your body it's night.

review.notes: Ordinary room-level light suppresses and delays melatonin in most people; 'can' keeps it appropriately hedged.

text: Sleeping in on the weekend can make Monday morning harder, because your internal clock has quietly shifted.

review.notes: Social jetlag, correctly described.

text: Your brain isn't idle while you sleep. Parts of it are as busy as they are when you're awake.
That thick fog right after waking has a name: sleep inertia. It happens when you surface out of a deep stage rather than a light one.

review.notes: Sleep inertia is worse on waking from slow-wave sleep; accurate.

text: Falling asleep depends on your body shedding heat, which is part of why a slightly cool room helps most people.

review.notes: measured claim 'most people' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Paper before bed tends to settle people more than a bright screen does. The light is part of it, and so is the fact that a book doesn't interrupt you.

review.notes: Hedged with 'tends to', and the light-emitting-eReader vs paper comparison supports both named mechanisms. Note the sleep-onset effect is modest (~10 minutes), so the text must not be firmed up in editing.

text: Most of your dreaming happens in the last stretch of a full night, which is why a short night cuts dreams more than anything else.

review.notes: measured claim 'Most of' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Your skin, muscle, and bone all repair faster while you're asleep than while you're up and about.

review.notes: Stated far more firmly than the evidence supports, and partly contradicted. Skin does not repair faster while you sleep: Hoyle et al. (Science Translational Medicine, 2017) found human burns sustained at night healed about 60% slower than daytime burns, because fibroblast mobilisation is circadian and peaks in the active phase. Overnight muscle protein synthesis is limited by amino acid availability rather than elevated by sleep per se, and bone resorption markers actually peak overnight. What is defensible is that poor or short sleep impairs repair — that is the claim to make, not a blanket 'skin, muscle and bone all repair faster while you're asleep'.

text: Almost nobody sleeps straight through. Brief wake-ups are normal, and you usually don't remember them by morning.

review.notes: Brief arousals are normal and usually unremembered; reassuring without being medical advice.

text: Deep inside each ear are tiny fluid-filled loops that sense when your head turns. That's your built-in balance sensor.

review.notes: Semicircular canals, correctly described for rotation; omitting the otoliths is a fair simplification.

text: Spinning makes you dizzy because that fluid keeps swirling for a few seconds after you've stopped.

review.notes: Endolymph inertia and cupula deflection; accurate.

text: Balance is a vote, not a single sense: your brain compares your eyes, your inner ears, and the pressure under your feet.

review.notes: Vision, vestibular and somatosensory integration; the 'vote' framing teaches the idea well.

text: Motion sickness happens when your eyes and your inner ears disagree about whether you're moving.

review.notes: Sensory conflict is the standard explanation used by major health bodies.

text: Your ankles handle the small wobbles when you're standing. Your hips take over once the wobble gets bigger.

review.notes: Ankle and hip postural strategies are established in the postural-control literature.

text: Looking at one fixed point makes balancing dramatically easier, because it gives your brain a reference to measure against.

review.notes: Visual fixation measurably improves postural stability.

text: Tightrope walkers carry a long pole because spreading mass out makes a body slower to tip — it buys them time to correct.

review.notes: Correct physics: a long pole raises rotational inertia, slowing the rate of tip.

text: Dancers avoid getting dizzy by spotting: snapping their head around to find the same point on every turn.

review.notes: Spotting is correctly described; 'avoid' is slightly absolute (dancers also habituate vestibularly) but not misleading.

text: The sense that tells you where your arm is without looking has a name — proprioception — and it's why you can touch your nose with your eyes shut.

review.notes: Proprioception, correctly named. The eyes-shut example is a seated finger-to-nose illustration, not an eyes-closed movement instruction, so it does not trip the safety rule.

text: Standing with your feet close together is much harder than standing with them apart. A wider base is simply more stable.

review.notes: measured claim 'harder than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Cats land on their feet using the same inner-ear system you have, just running much faster.

review.notes: Misattributes the cat righting reflex to a 'faster' inner ear. The vestibular system only triggers the reflex — humans have that part too and it is not the limiting factor. What lets a cat land on its feet is body mechanics: an unusually flexible spine and no functional collarbone, letting it counter-rotate front and back halves and reorient while conserving angular momentum. As written it teaches the wrong cause.

text: Your center of gravity sits roughly behind your belly button, and every movement you make shifts it somewhere new.

review.notes: Whole-body centre of mass sits roughly at navel level (anterior to S2); 'roughly' carries the approximation honestly.

text: Sailors get their sea legs because the brain learns to expect the ship's motion — and then has to unlearn it once they're back on land.

review.notes: Sensorimotor adaptation to ship motion and the readaptation on land are well described; the claim is hedged at the right level and teaches a real mechanism.

text: Carrying a tray of full cups trains balance in a way standing still never can, because the load keeps moving on you.

review.notes: "in a way standing still never can" is an absolute nobody measured, and the underlying claim that carrying a tray trains balance is asserted, not evidenced. Drop the absolute and state it as a plausible difference in demand, not a training effect.

text: Balancing on one foot while you brush your teeth turns two minutes you already spend into two minutes of practice.

review.notes: Safety: a single-leg stand at a bathroom sink, on a hard and often wet floor, is suggested to an audience that includes seniors, with no mention of keeping a hand near the counter and no naming of the fall risk. Also frames it as "two minutes of practice" when nobody balances on one foot for the full two minutes.

text: Children's balance keeps developing for years after they learn to walk. It isn't finished at toddlerhood.

review.notes: Postural control continues maturing well past toddlerhood into adolescence. True, correctly unquantified, and useful for a young reader.

text: The same weight is easier to balance split between two hands than carried in one.

review.notes: Symmetric loading keeps the centre of mass closer to the base of support; a one-sided load forces trunk compensation. True at this level of detail, no overclaim.

text: Thin soles let your feet feel more of the ground, which is part of why balancing barefoot on a firm floor feels steadier.

review.notes: Plantar cutaneous feedback is a genuine contributor to postural control, and the item hedges honestly ("part of why", "feels steadier") rather than claiming barefoot is measurably better.

text: Balance takes more practice to hold on to as the years go by, which is exactly what makes a minute of it worth spending.

review.notes: Age-related decline in balance is well established; the second clause is an explicit value judgement about spending a minute, not a dose or sufficiency claim.

text: Every step you take is a brief moment of balancing on one leg. You've done it so often you stopped noticing.

review.notes: Single-support phase of gait is real and this reframes something familiar without overstating it.

text: Most of the tightness you feel in a stretch is your nervous system putting the brakes on, not the muscle running out of length.

review.notes: Firmness. "Most of the tightness" is a proportion nobody measured, and the mechanism is actively argued: current reviews find both reduced passive stiffness and increased stretch tolerance contribute, with tolerance dominant only over longer training periods. Either hedge ("a lot of what you feel is...") or mark contested and say the question is open.

text: That's why you can often reach further on the third try than the first — your body has decided the position is safe.

review.notes: Two defects. It opens with "That's why", a dangling referent to SF-FCT-000190 that breaks when the item is served on its own, which is how this library is read. And "your body has decided the position is safe" is a vivid causal mechanism stated as fact for an acute effect whose cause is not settled.

text: Your hamstrings cross both your knee and your hip, which is why bending forward feels completely different with a straight leg than a bent one.

review.notes: Hamstrings are biarticular and hip/knee position genuinely changes what a forward bend loads. Accurate and explanatory.

text: Sitting keeps the muscles at the front of your hips in a shortened position for hours, which is a lot of why standing up feels stiff.

review.notes: "a lot of why" is an unmeasured proportion, and "shortened position" is the weakest-supported version of this claim. Evidence supports increased passive hip-flexor stiffness and reduced hip extension after prolonged sitting, not structural shortening; no study links length of sitting to hip flexor tightness directly. Rewrite as stiffness, and drop the proportion.

text: Joints are built with different ranges on purpose: your shoulder can circle all the way around, your elbow only bends one way.

review.notes: Correct contrast between a multiaxial and a uniaxial joint, and the "on purpose" framing teaches the trade-off rather than just naming parts.

text: Your shoulder is the most mobile joint you have, and that freedom is exactly why it depends so much on the muscles around it.

review.notes: The glenohumeral joint being the most mobile joint in the body is standard anatomy, and the mobility/stability trade-off is correctly stated.

text: Bouncing at the end of a stretch is less controlled than easing into it, which is mostly why it's discouraged — the range you gain looks much the same either way.

review.notes: Both halves are wrong in a safety-relevant direction. Ballistic stretching is discouraged primarily for injury risk, not merely because it is "less controlled", and the item explicitly downplays that. And "the range you gain looks much the same either way" is contradicted: meta-analytic comparisons put ballistic stretching's effect on range of motion below static and PNF. Telling a nine-year-old that bouncing gets the same result is the opposite of the guideline.

text: Some people are naturally more flexible because of how their connective tissue is built, not because they practiced more.

review.notes: Individual variation in connective tissue and joint laxity is real, and "some people" keeps it appropriately unquantified. Also usefully defuses comparison between bodies.

text: Breathing out as you settle into a stretch usually lets you sink a little further. Holding your breath does the opposite.

review.notes: The exhale-lets-you-sink-further claim is gym folklore stated as fact ("usually"), with no good evidence behind it, and "Holding your breath does the opposite" invents a matching effect. It also introduces breath-holding as a technique to a nine-year-old audience, which the safety rules avoid. Cut the breath-holding half or reframe the whole item as relaxation, not range.

text: Moving stretches — arm circles, leg swings — prepare you for activity better than holding still ones do.

review.notes: reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'better than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Mild tension means a stretch is doing its job. Anything sharp is a different signal entirely.

review.notes: Distinguishing stretch tension from sharp pain is exactly the right safety cue for this audience, and it is stated without diagnosing anything.

text: Your spine is a stack of small bones that each move only slightly. The big bend you can see is all of them adding up.

review.notes: Accurate description of segmental spinal motion summing to gross range. Teaches something a reader will not have pictured.

text: Your calves connect to your heel through the thickest tendon in your body.

review.notes: Verified: the Achilles is described in the anatomical literature as the thickest and strongest tendon in the body, formed from gastrocnemius and soleus and inserting on the calcaneus.

text: Cats, dogs, and people all stretch the moment they get up. The reflex is old enough to have its own name: pandiculation.

review.notes: Pandiculation is a real, widely observed vertebrate behaviour and naming it is worth the reader's attention. The "old enough to have its own name" line is a loose flourish but makes no health claim.

text: Reaching straight overhead stretches muscles running all the way down your side to your lower back, not just your arm.

review.notes: Latissimus dorsi runs from the humerus to the thoracolumbar fascia and lower spine, so an overhead reach does load far more than the arm. Accurate.

text: One of your hip muscles starts at your lower spine and crosses all the way to your thigh — a long way for a single muscle to travel.

review.notes: Accurate description of psoas major, correctly left unnamed for a nine-year-old, and the length of the muscle is genuinely surprising.

text: Flexibility is joint by joint. Loose shoulders tell you almost nothing about your hips.

review.notes: "almost nothing" is an overstatement and it contradicts SF-FCT-000197 in this same packet: generalised connective-tissue laxity is precisely why hypermobility is scored across multiple joints. Joint specificity is real; the strength of the claim is not. Soften to "tell you less than you would think".

text: Yoga and plain old stretching improve flexibility through the same mechanism: regular, unhurried time spent at the end of your range.

review.notes: "the same mechanism" is an unearned identity claim between two practices that have not been shown to work identically, and what follows the colon is a description of practice (regular time at end range), not a mechanism. Restate as "work the same way in practice" or cut the mechanism framing.

text: The stretch you do without thinking when you wake up is one your body asked for on its own.

review.notes: Quality failure. It restates SF-FCT-000203 with the content removed and teaches nothing checkable; "one your body asked for on its own" is a phrase, not a fact. Either fold into the pandiculation item or give it real content.

text: Knees and elbows are hinges, wrists and ankles are closer to universal joints. The same stretch can't possibly suit all of them.

review.notes: Anatomically wrong: the ankle (talocrural) joint is classified as a uniaxial hinge, the same category as the knee and elbow; the side-to-side motion comes from the subtalar joint below it. "universal joints" is also not a standard classification for the wrist, which is condyloid. And "can't possibly suit all of them" is an overclaim on top of the error.

text: Habits live in a different part of the brain than decisions do, which is why a routine eventually stops needing willpower.

review.notes: Stated more firmly than the neuroscience supports. The clean prefrontal-to-striatum handoff is the old account; current work finds both systems remain active and compete rather than one replacing the other, and cortical involvement is task-dependent. "stops needing willpower" also overstates automaticity. Should be hedged or marked contested.

text: Starting is nearly always harder than continuing. Most people feel better a few minutes in than they did at the door.

review.notes: Two proportions nobody measured: "nearly always" and "Most people feel better a few minutes in". There is real work on people mispredicting how exercise will feel, but not at this firmness. Label editorial or hedge to "often".

text: Every habit needs a cue, and the most reliable cue is something already nailed down in your day, like brushing your teeth.

review.notes: An absolute and a superlative in one sentence. "Every habit needs a cue" is stated as a law, and "the most reliable cue is" ranks cue types against each other on no measurement — existing-routine anchoring is supported as effective, not as most reliable.

text: Writing down exactly when and where you'll do something makes it noticeably more likely to actually happen.

review.notes: Implementation intentions are among the better-replicated findings in this area, and "noticeably more likely" is hedged correctly rather than quoting an effect size the item cannot source.

text: Making something easier to start beats trying harder to want it.

review.notes: "beats" is a head-to-head comparative between two approaches that have not been compared head to head. It is also advice, not a simplified fact, so the confidence label is wrong — SF-FCT-000220 shows `editorial` is available and unused here.

text: Your brain remembers the end of an experience more strongly than the middle, so finishing on a good note is what pulls you back.

review.notes: Misstates the peak-end rule: it is peak AND end that dominate retrospective evaluation, and this item drops the peak entirely. "is what pulls you back" then asserts a single cause for return behaviour that the evidence supports only as one predictor among several.

text: Getting back to it on day two matters far more than being perfect on day one.

review.notes: "far more" is an unmeasured comparative. The defensible version — missing a single day does not derail habit formation — is worth saying, but not with a magnitude attached, and this is editorial rather than simplified.

text: Streaks work because they turn something abstract into something you can see at a glance.

review.notes: "Streaks work because" asserts a mechanism for the app's own core feature with nothing behind it, and picks one explanation (visibility) over the more obvious ones (loss aversion, commitment). Either hedge to "part of why streaks work" or mark it editorial and own it as a product opinion.

text: Tracking anything tends to change it, purely because you're now paying attention to it.

review.notes: The reactivity of self-monitoring is a real effect, but "purely because you're now paying attention to it" is a mechanism overclaim — tracking also changes what people choose to do because they know it will be recorded. Drop "purely".

text: The friction between you and a habit is usually physical: where the shoes are, whether the bag is packed, how far the mat is.

review.notes: "usually physical" is an unmeasured proportion and is likely wrong: the barriers people report most are time, fatigue and how they expect it to feel, not where the shoes are. The examples are good; the ranking claim is not earned.

text: Most people find it easier to keep a promise made to someone else than one made only to themselves.

review.notes: reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'Most people' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: A habit tied to a time of day holds up better than one tied to a mood.

review.notes: "holds up better" is presented as a finding but is a comparative nobody measured. Cue consistency is supported in general; time-of-day versus mood specifically is not. Hedge or relabel editorial.

text: Deciding in advance is how you avoid having the argument with yourself later.

review.notes: Plainly advice in advice voice, sound, safe, and consistent with the implementation-intention literature without claiming to be a measurement.

text: Rewards stick best when they arrive right after the thing you did, not weeks down the line.

review.notes: Reward immediacy is a well-supported principle of learning, and "stick best" here refers to a genuine and large timing effect rather than an invented ranking.

text: The clearest sign a habit has taken hold is that skipping it starts to feel strange.

review.notes: "The clearest sign" is an unearned superlative. Reduced conscious deliberation and a sense of oddity when skipping are indicators of automaticity, but nothing establishes this as the clearest one. "A good sign" fixes it.

text: Big goals are useful for pointing the direction. Only the small daily version is something you can actually do today.

review.notes: A clean, safe framing that moves attention from outcome goals to today's action, with no empirical claim to overstate.

text: Changing your surroundings changes your behavior faster than changing your mind does.

review.notes: "faster than changing your mind does" is a speed comparison between two things never measured against each other. The environment-shapes-behaviour point survives without the race.

text: People are reliably poor at guessing how much they'll get done in a week. The usual direction of the error is too much.

review.notes: Planning fallacy, correctly stated including the direction of the error (people overestimate what they will finish). Hedged with 'reliably poor' rather than a made-up percentage. Age-appropriate and useful.

text: A smaller version of a habit still counts. A sloppier one is worth watching, though — repetition sets whatever pattern you repeat.

review.notes: Small-dose habit framing is consistent with the app's values and safe; the second clause (repetition ingrains whatever pattern is repeated) is ordinary motor-learning and is stated without a fake number. Teaches something real about form.

text: Having a plan for the day you don't feel like it is what keeps most streaks alive.

review.notes: Firmness defect. 'is what keeps MOST streaks alive' is an unearned proportion — nobody measured what keeps most streaks alive. The underlying idea (implementation intentions / if-then plans help adherence) is supported, but it is stated as a measured majority. Soften to something like 'Deciding in advance what you'll do on the day you don't feel like it is one of the things that keeps a streak alive.'

text: Kids move most when nobody calls it exercise. Call the same thing a game and it tends to go on considerably longer.

review.notes: Two unearned comparatives in one item: 'Kids move most when nobody calls it exercise' (superlative) and 'tends to go on considerably longer' (a quantified duration comparison nobody measured here). The core observation — framing activity as play rather than exercise raises engagement — is plausible but is stated far more firmly than any cited evidence. Also `simplified` with no source for what is really a behavioural research claim.

text: Given time, space, and no instructions, most children move on their own. Play does the work that a plan can't.

review.notes: Hedged ('most children', 'given time, space, and no instructions'), safe, and true of free play at the level of detail given. The closing line is editorial colour rather than a factual overreach.

text: Walking side by side often makes a hard conversation easier than sitting across a table for it.

review.notes: Properly hedged with 'often'. Side-by-side walking reducing the pressure of a hard conversation is a modest, non-medical claim and is not stated as a measured effect. Safe for all ages.

text: When one person in a household changes a routine, the people around them usually drift a little in the same direction.

review.notes: Household behaviour concordance is real and the item hedges twice ('usually', 'a little'). No mechanism is invented and no proportion is claimed.

text: Younger siblings tend to want whatever the older ones are doing, which quietly turns big brothers and sisters into coaches.

review.notes: Sibling modelling is well documented, and the claim is hedged with 'tend to'. The 'coaches' line is framing, not an invented effect. Safe and age-appropriate.

text: Doing the same thing on the same day each week turns it into a landmark that kids still remember years later.

review.notes: Stated as a guaranteed outcome: a weekly repeat 'turns it into a landmark that kids still remember years later.' Family-ritual research supports that rituals are valued and remembered, but not that repeating anything weekly reliably produces a decades-long memory. Needs a hedge ('can become', 'often') rather than a promise.

text: Letting a child choose the activity makes them far more likely to want to do it again.

review.notes: 'far more likely' is an unearned magnitude. Choice/autonomy does support intrinsic motivation, but the size of the effect here is invented. Drop 'far' or cite the autonomy-support evidence.

text: Carrying groceries, pushing a stroller, walking the dog — a lot of family life is already movement that nobody bothered to label.

review.notes: Straightforwardly true (incidental daily activity is real movement), no number claimed, safe, and it usefully reframes existing activity without any body or weight framing.

text: Racing a kid to the end of the street gives you both a sprint, and only one of you will call it a workout.

review.notes: Safety. The item invites a nine-year-old to race 'to the end of the street' and does not name the traffic hazard, which the rubric requires for anything a child could copy and be hurt by. Relocate it to a safe setting (park, yard, path) or name the condition explicitly.

text: Grandparents moving alongside grandkids show them something no explanation can: what staying active for decades looks like.

review.notes: Warm, safe, non-comparative, and makes a genuine point about modelling across generations. No factual claim to overreach on.

text: Cheering for someone works better than comparing them to someone.

review.notes: reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'better than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Chores that involve lifting and carrying are real movement. They just arrive with a to-do list attached.

review.notes: True, safe, and it reframes chores as movement without any weight or body-composition framing. Modest but it does teach the reframe.

text: Kids usually have more stamina for play than adults expect and less patience for repeating the same thing.

review.notes: Hedged with 'usually' and framed against adult expectation rather than as a measurement. Children being more fatigue-resistant in intermittent play is well supported, and the boredom half is plainly observational.

text: A family can move at different speeds and still move together. The slowest person sets the pace, and that's the whole point.

review.notes: Inclusive, safe, no comparison of bodies, and it makes a real point about pacing a group. Nothing to verify and nothing overstated.

text: Movement is one of the few things a nine-year-old and a sixty-year-old can genuinely do side by side.

review.notes: 'one of the few things' is an unearned superlative and is easy to falsify — a nine-year-old and a sixty-year-old can genuinely cook, play games, garden or make music side by side too. The point survives without the ranking: say movement is one of the things they can do side by side at their own speeds.

text: Telling someone what you did today is often the thing that gets them to do it tomorrow.

review.notes: Hedged with 'often', and the accountability/telling-someone effect is a reasonable, non-medical claim. No proportion or magnitude invented.

text: Dogs are the most reliable exercise partners in most households, mainly because they ask every single day.

review.notes: Three firmness problems stacked: 'the MOST reliable exercise partners', 'in MOST households', and the causal 'mainly because'. None of that is measured, and the dog-walking literature is actually mixed — a large share of dog owners do not walk their dog regularly. Rewrite as an observation about the daily prompt a dog provides, without the superlative or the household proportion.

text: An hour on a playground teaches balance, coordination, and nerve. None of it looks like training to the kid doing it.

review.notes: True and non-quantified: playground play does develop balance, coordination and confidence. Safe, and the closing point (it doesn't feel like training) is the actual insight.

text: The habit a child watches an adult keep on a bad day is the one that sticks.

review.notes: Correctly labelled `editorial`, which licenses the firmness of 'is the one that sticks'. Safe, no medical claim, and it says something worth reading to an adult user.

text: Adults tend to underestimate how closely kids watch what they do, and overestimate how much they hear what they're told.

review.notes: Hedged with 'tend to' on both halves and framed as a comparison against adults' own expectations rather than a measured quantity. Consistent with modelling research.

text: There are no muscles inside your fingers. They're pulled by tendons running from your forearm, like puppet strings.

review.notes: Verified anatomy: the fingers contain no muscle bellies; flexion and extension come from extrinsic forearm muscles acting through long tendons. The puppet-string image is an accurate simplification, not an invented mechanism.

text: There are 26 bones in each foot — about a quarter of your skeleton, in the two parts of you that touch the ground.

review.notes: Verified: 26 bones per foot, 52 of roughly 206 bones, which is genuinely about a quarter. The proportion is one of the few in this packet that is actually arithmetic rather than assertion.

text: The three smallest bones in your body are in your ear, and all three together would sit comfortably on a fingernail.

review.notes: Verified: the malleus, incus and stapes are the smallest bones in the body, the largest about 8 mm. 'All three on a fingernail' is a fair size image, not an invented measurement.

text: Your thigh bone is the longest and strongest bone you have, and it's slightly curved rather than straight.

review.notes: Verified: the femur is the longest and strongest bone, and its anterior bow (a real, named feature) is correctly described as a slight curve rather than straight. Good detail that most readers won't know.

text: Nobody has fully explained why we yawn, but it's reliably contagious — reading this sentence is often enough to start one.

review.notes: Verified on both halves: the function of yawning genuinely is unresolved (and the item says so, which is the honest handling of an open question), and reading or thinking about yawning is a documented contagion trigger. 'Often' is the right hedge.

text: You have more than six hundred muscles, and standing up out of a chair uses dozens of them at once.

review.notes: reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'more than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Your eyes never truly hold still. Even when you're staring at one spot, they're making tiny jumps you can't feel.

review.notes: Microsaccades and fixational drift are established and the item claims nothing beyond their existence and imperceptibility. Genuinely surprising to a reader, which is what this category is for.

text: Your left lung has two lobes and your right has three. The left gave up a lobe's worth of space to the heart.

review.notes: Verified: two lobes on the left, three on the right, and the left lung's cardiac notch really is the heart occupying that space. The 'gave up a lobe's worth of space' phrasing is a simplification of standard anatomy, not an invented mechanism.

text: A drop of blood makes a full circuit of your body in about a minute.

review.notes: 'About a minute' is the mainstream resting figure (roughly 5 L blood over roughly 5 L/min cardiac output); published estimates run 20-60 seconds, so 'about a minute' is within range and appropriately approximate.

text: The blood vessels in one adult body, laid end to end, would stretch tens of thousands of miles.

review.notes: 'Tens of thousands of miles' is the correctly loose version of the commonly cited 60,000-mile estimate — notably, the item did NOT commit to the precise figure, which is the right call given the estimate's softness.

text: Nerve signals travel from your brain to your muscles faster than a car moves on the highway.

review.notes: reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'faster than' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Your bones are alive. They have blood vessels and nerves, and they're being taken apart and rebuilt continuously.

review.notes: Established bone biology — vascularised, innervated, continuously remodelled — stated without any dose, rate or proportion. Corrects a real misconception children hold.

text: Everyone has muscles around their ears, but only some people can actually wiggle them on command.

review.notes: Verified: the auricular muscles are present in everyone and voluntary control is variable. Stated with the correct hedge ('only some people'), no proportion invented.

text: The bumps you can see on your tongue aren't taste buds. The taste buds are tucked along the sides of those bumps.

review.notes: Verified and non-obvious: the visible lingual papillae are not themselves taste buds; the buds sit in the epithelium along the papillae's walls. A genuine correction of a common misconception.

text: Your sense of smell does most of the work you credit to your tongue, which is why food tastes flat with a blocked nose.

review.notes: reviewer accepted, but measured claim 'most of' with no sources — a comparative, proportion or dose needs one whatever the confidence tier says; hedge it or cite it

text: Your eyes shut when you sneeze, and it takes real effort to stop them. Nobody has fully explained what the reflex is for.

review.notes: Both citations are real but neither one addresses the claim at all -- this is the same-general-topic failure, not genuine support. PMC8663001 is 'Experimental measurements of airflow features and velocity distribution exhaled from sneeze and speech using particle image velocimetry' (Building and Environment): it measures sneeze airflow velocity for virus-transmission modelling and contains nothing about the eye-closing reflex. The PopSci piece 'FYI: How Forceful Is A Sneeze?' is likewise entirely about sneeze velocity and the Wells 224 mph myth, and does not mention eyes. So an item marked confidence 'established' currently has zero support for either of its two sentences, including the notable 'nobody has fully explained what the reflex is for'. The underlying claim appears true and is safe for a nine-year-old, so this is salvageable -- but it must be re-sourced to literature that actually covers the sneeze blink reflex before it can stay labelled 'established'. These two velocity citations look like they were copy-pasted from SF-FCT-000084.

text: Your brain uses about a fifth of all the energy your body spends, even when you're sitting perfectly still.

review.notes: 'About a fifth' matches the standard ~20% of resting metabolic rate for the brain, and the 'even when sitting still' clause is the correct and interesting part.

text: Astronauts grow an inch or two in orbit. There's plenty of gravity up there — they're just falling around the Earth, so nothing is pressing their spine together.

review.notes: Verified against NASA: spinal lengthening in microgravity is commonly cited as up to about 3%, roughly two inches for a tall adult, so 'an inch or two' is accurate. The item also actively corrects the 'no gravity in space' misconception with the right explanation (free fall), which is a bonus rather than a defect.

text: Humans are the best long-distance runners in the animal kingdom. Not because we're fast — because we sweat, and most animals can only cool down by panting, which they can't do while galloping.

review.notes: Both URLs resolve, but the item is stated far more firmly than either source supports, and its own citation contradicts the 'established' label. (1) The Wikipedia endurance running hypothesis article explicitly presents this as a debated hypothesis and carries an 'Academic discourse' section recording that the proposed traits were called 'trivial' or 'incorrect' and that most remain untested; an item whose primary source labels the idea contested cannot be served as confidence 'established'.
