(2) Neither source says humans are 'the best long-distance runners in the animal kingdom'. Wikipedia makes the far narrower claim that 'no primates other than humans are capable of endurance running'; the UC Davis blog 'Humans are Born to Run' says only 'we may not be the best sprinters in the animal kingdom, we can run steadily for long distances, even in hot weather'. The superlative is the item's own invention, and it is disputed -- sled dogs, horses, camels and pronghorn are routinely cited as matching or beating humans over distance. (3) The mechanism sentence -- 'most animals can only cool down by panting, which they can't do while galloping' -- appears in neither source. The UC Davis page does not discuss panting while galloping at all, and Wikipedia explicitly does not. As stated it is also wrong: respiratory-locomotor coupling constrains a galloping quadruped's breathing, it does not make panting impossible, and horses and camels sweat substantially. Fix by reframing as the contested hypothesis it is ('one idea about why humans are unusually good at running in the heat'), setting confidence to 'contested' with the text saying so, dropping the superlative, and sourcing the panting claim to real physiology or cutting it.

text: Fingernails grow faster than toenails, and the nails on your dominant hand grow fastest of all.

review.notes: Firmness defect of exactly the type this library has. The first half (fingernails grow faster than toenails) is solidly established; the second half — 'the nails on your dominant hand grow fastest of all' — is stated flatly as fact when the evidence is mixed: it rests largely on Bean's decades-long self-observation, and at least one peer-reviewed comparison found no significant right/left difference. Either drop the dominant-hand clause or mark it as something people have noticed but not settled.

text: Bouncing back from something hard isn't about not finding it hard. It's about what you do in the days after.

review.notes: Safe, non-clinical resilience framing that explicitly refuses to tell a reader they shouldn't find hard things hard. No mechanism, dose or proportion claimed.

text: Sleep is the least glamorous form of looking after yourself and the one that changes the most.

review.notes: 'the one that changes the most' is an unearned superlative, ranking sleep above every other self-care behaviour with nothing to support the ranking. Sleep's importance is not in doubt; the league table is. Rewrite without the ranking, e.g. 'and one of the ones that changes the most.'

text: In a disagreement, saying how you feel and then actually listening gets further than either silence or scorekeeping.

review.notes: Safe, age-appropriate conflict guidance with no medical or psychological claim beyond common sense. Nothing to overstate.

text: Gratitude isn't pretending things are fine. It's noticing the parts that already are.

review.notes: Defines gratitude honestly and explicitly rules out toxic positivity ('isn't pretending things are fine'), which is the right handling for a young audience. No claim about outcomes or benefits, so nothing to overreach.

text: Asking for help is a normal thing that people do, not evidence that something has gone wrong with you.

review.notes: Editorial, correctly labelled, safe, non-shaming, and useful to a 9-year-old. No factual claim to overstate.

text: Moving regularly is linked to steadier mood, not just a healthier body — and short counts.

review.notes: Correctly hedged ('is linked to'), and 'short counts' is supported by the physical-activity/mood literature. Simplified label is honest here.

text: Talk to yourself after a mistake the way you'd talk to a friend who made it. Most people are far harsher with themselves than they would ever be out loud.

review.notes: 'Most people are far harsher with themselves than they would ever be out loud' states a measured-sounding proportion and comparative that nobody has measured. The advice is fine; soften to 'many people' or drop the quantifier.

text: Being tired and short-tempered for days at a time is usually a request for rest rather than a character flaw.

review.notes: Quasi-medical reassurance: days of tiredness plus irritability is a symptom pattern with many causes (illness, low mood, poor sleep, anaemia), and 'usually a request for rest' is a firmness claim with no source, aimed at 9-year-olds. Either reframe as 'often worth treating as a rest signal' plus 'if it keeps going, tell someone', or drop it.

text: When someone is upset, being listened to helps sooner than being fixed.

review.notes: Qualitative, safe, consistent with validation/emotion-regulation research, and appropriate at min_age 9.

text: A boundary is just being honest about what you can take on. It doesn't need a reason attached to it.

review.notes: Mislabelled: this is an editorial stance on boundaries, not a 'simplified' factual claim with detail left out. Also 'It doesn't need a reason attached to it' is delivered unqualified to a nine-year-old, where it can read as licence to refuse a caregiver without explanation. Relabel editorial and add the relationship context.

text: A few minutes outside in the middle of a bad day is a reset that costs nothing and works more often than it should.

review.notes: Self-aware hedging ('works more often than it should') keeps the firmness honest, and going outside is safe. Note it overlaps heavily with SF-FCT-000287.

text: Small wins are worth noticing out loud. Motivation is built from the ones you bothered to count.

review.notes: Editorial, correctly labelled, safe, and on-message without claiming anything measurable.

text: A pause before you answer, when you're angry, is the difference between responding and reacting.

review.notes: Essentially definitional (responding vs reacting) and safe; the 'simplified' label is loose but the statement does not overreach.

text: Relationships are built from showing up in small ways repeatedly, not from occasional grand gestures.

review.notes: Editorial, correctly labelled, safe, and a genuine idea rather than a platitude.

text: Looking after yourself is mostly maintenance — sleep, food, movement, rest. The expensive version is optional.

review.notes: Safe, non-commercial, no meal-skipping or body-composition framing, and it teaches something real about what self-care actually is.

text: Comparing yourself to someone else is a normal thing your brain does. Noticing it is what lets you put it down.

review.notes: Social comparison being automatic is well supported, and the item does not shame the reader for it. 'Noticing it is what lets you put it down' is a slightly firm mechanism but stays within simplified.

text: When you feel left out, reaching out to one person usually helps more than working out why you were left out.

review.notes: Editorial and correctly labelled; the comparative is qualitative, not a fabricated measurement, and the advice is safe.

text: Time outside lifts mood and lowers stress at any age, in any season, and it doesn't take long.

review.notes: 'at any age, in any season, and it doesn't take long' is an unearned universal. The nature-exposure evidence is mostly temperate-season adult samples with modest effects; drop the 'any age, any season' absolutism. Also near-duplicates SF-FCT-000280.
